one_line: A scrolling fashion quarterly for OUR TIME in which time is the filing system — every image carries a real dateline, the collection is sorted chronologically before it is sorted by category, and the page opens on "EARN EVERY SECOND." and closes on "OUR TIME.", with the only moving thing on the site being a single slow specular sweep across the glass pill, one revolution per page.
big_idea:
**The site is a printed lookbook that happens to scroll, and the thing it is a record OF is time.**

Most "time-themed" sites reach for clocks, sand and countdowns — decoration. This one treats time the way a magazine treats it: as the **dateline**. Every image on the site carries a small mono caption with a real date and a real place. Every product carries the date it was made and the drop it belongs to. The collection page defaults to chronological order — newest first, a ledger — and *category is a filter applied on top of that*. Time is the spine of the information architecture, not the wallpaper. That single decision is what lets us throw away every clock-face cliché and still be the most time-obsessed site in the category.

Why it fits OUR TIME specifically, and nothing else:

1. **The corrected name gives us a two-act narrative and the site is structured as those two acts.** The grind register ("EARN EVERY SECOND.", "TIME WON'T WAIT.", "DISCIPLINE. FOCUS. CONSISTENCY.") owns the top of the home page. The arrival register ("OUR TIME.") is held back and spent exactly once, at the bottom, after the hourglass has filled. Put in the overtime, then it's our time. You cannot scroll this page without experiencing that arc, and no other brand can use it because no other brand is called this.

2. **"OUR" is collective, so the site never addresses a single reader.** No "you". No hustle-grind lone-wolf copy. The connective writing is in "we", and the one about page is 220 words with no founder portrait, no team grid, no stats band. The crowd is implied by the photography — two models, same location, same light, repeatedly — rather than stated.

3. **Editorial restraint is the only register that survives AI imagery.** The failure mode of AI fashion photography is uncanny faces, plastic skin, and symmetrical front-on portraits. The failure mode of ALD/Jacquemus-grade art direction is *backs turned, cropped at the jaw, mid-stride, overcast light, one enormous image with nothing on it*. Those are the same picture. The brand's aesthetic requirement and the model's technical weakness point in the same direction, which is rare and should be exploited ruthlessly.

4. **The hourglass back-print is the best asset in the range, so the site's one expensive moment is built from it.** The single pinned canvas sequence — the only piece of real motion on the site — is the hourglass's *lower* bulb filling, Blender-rendered, 120 frames, as the home page ends. Accrual, not depletion. The garment print and the site's structural climax are the same object, which is what makes it read as a brand rather than a template with a nice background.

5. **The liquid glass earns its place by being the only UI on the page.** There is no header band, no scroll indicator, no breadcrumb, no section eyebrow, no card chrome, no shadows. One floating pill, four words in it, and a slow raking highlight that crosses it once per page like a hand crossing a dial. When it is the only jewellery, it can afford to be jewellery.

art_direction.palette:
Tokens are taken from the measured render values and nothing is invented. No new hue enters the brand from the website — the accent is a garment colour.

GROUND / DARK THEME
- `--ot-ground` **#0F0F0F** — the dark page. Never #000000. Pure black is reserved for the photographic backdrop *inside* images, which is how the images read as lit objects sitting on a page rather than holes cut in it.
- `--ot-ink` **#FAF6F6** — bone ink on dark (the logo white, slightly warm). 17.9:1 on ground.
- `--ot-ink-quiet` **#A7A5A4** — washed grey, used for mono datelines, captions, sold-out state, secondary nav. 7.7:1 on ground, so it is legible at 10px, which matters because that is where it lives.
- `--ot-rule-dark` **rgb(250 246 246 / .14)** — hairlines on dark. 1px, never 2.

PAPER / LIGHT THEME (collection, product, cart, index spread)
- `--ot-paper` **#DFDDDE** — off-white. The light page is paper-toned, not white; nothing on this site is #FFFFFF.
- `--ot-paper-warm` **#CFC2B4** — cream/sand. Used on exactly one surface: the closing colophon band. It is the warmest note on the site and it arrives last, after the hourglass, which is the point.
- `--ot-ink-dark` **#141B2C** — the navy tee colour, used as **ink on paper**. Body copy on the light theme is navy, not black. 12.8:1 on paper. This is the single most fashion-house decision in the palette and it costs nothing.
- `--ot-rule-light` **rgb(20 27 44 / .18)**.

ACCENT — one only
- `--ot-denim` **#54647E** — washed denim. The most saturated thing the brand owns, so introducing anything louder would instantly become the brand's loudest colour. Permitted uses, exhaustively: the selected/active state on size and colour selectors under the light theme; the 1px rule under an applied filter chip; the underline on inline text links on paper. Never a button fill, never on the dark theme, never a glow.

PRODUCT COLOURS (image content, never UI surfaces)
#141B2C navy tee · #141925 navy short · #171717 washed black · #A7A5A4 washed grey · #54647E washed denim · #DFDDDE off-white · #CFC2B4 cream/sand. Forest green and brown/taupe join later.

TWO HARD CONSTRAINTS THAT FALL OUT OF THE MEASUREMENTS
- **Washed black #171717 can never be photographed or displayed against #0F0F0F or #000000** — 8 points of luminance apart, the garment vanishes. Washed black pieces are shot on paper (#DFDDDE) or on a mid-grey sweep, always. This is a shot-list rule, not a CSS rule.
- **Washed grey #A7A5A4 against paper #DFDDDE is 1.84:1** — the grey shorts disappear on the light theme with no shadow to save them. Washed grey is shot on the dark ground only. Enforce in the catalogue as a `bg` field per colourway so the grid never places a garment on a background it dies against.

FOCUS RING (works on both themes, no new colour): `outline: 2px solid #FAF6F6; outline-offset: 2px; box-shadow: 0 0 0 4px #0F0F0F;` on dark, and the two colours swapped on paper. Solid, never translucent, always painted above the glass.
art_direction.typography:
**One superfamily, three registers, four styles. No serif. No Google font.**

The brand's display voice is already the heavy italic OT monogram — a serif would fight it, and the thin wide wordmark cannot carry a headline. So the contrast comes from **width and scale**, not from a second personality.

PRIMARY RECOMMENDATION — Klim Type Foundry, self-hosted woff2
- **Söhne Schmal, Kräftig** — display. Narrow Swiss grotesque with real authority at 100px. All headlines, all display.
- **Söhne, Buch (400) + Kräftig (500)** — body, nav, buttons, product copy.
- **Söhne Mono, Buch** — the metadata layer: datelines, drop codes, SKUs, sizes, colour names, measurements, the countdown digits' legends. This is where the time theme lives typographically.
*Licensing:* Klim webfont licences are perpetual and banded by monthly pageviews; at a launch tier (≤250k/mo) budget roughly **£450–£700 for four styles**, one-off, self-hosted, no CDN call, no third-party tracking. Verify the current band on klim.co.nz before purchase. Söhne is what Aimé Leon Dore ships, so it is proven in exactly this register — the differentiation is in the *system*, not in owning a rare face.

BUDGET ALTERNATIVE (if Klim is a no) — Pangram Pangram, one-off, webfont included with desktop, no pageview metering, roughly **£100–£250 per family**
- Display: **PP Right Grotesk Compact, Medium**
- Text: **PP Neue Montreal, Book + Medium**
- Data: **PP Fraktion Mono, Regular**

ZERO-BUDGET FLOOR (ship-able, not preferred): `-apple-system, "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial` for display and text (the Stüssy position — three weights of Helvetica Neue and nothing else), **IBM Plex Mono** for data. **Banned outright: Inter, Poppins, Montserrat, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Raleway, Nunito, DM Sans, Manrope, Space Grotesk, Plus Jakarta Sans.** Trapstar and Kith both ship Inter as heading *and* body and both look generated; this is not a theoretical risk.

THE WORDMARK IS NOT A WEBFONT
"OUR TIME" is delivered as **inline SVG with outlined paths**, from the supplied art, so the word space is geometry and cannot collapse. `<svg role="img" aria-label="Our Time">` with a `<title>`. It appears **exactly twice on the entire site**: the colophon lockup and the first-paint state. Nowhere else, ever.

Where the two words must be set in live type (the `<title>` tag, the OG image, the newsletter footer line), protect the gap explicitly and never trust a default:
```css
.ot-wordmark-type{font-family:"Sohne",sans-serif;font-weight:300;text-transform:uppercase;
  letter-spacing:.34em;word-spacing:.62em;white-space:nowrap;padding-right:.34em}
```
The trailing `padding-right` compensates the final letter's tracking space so the lockup optically centres. `word-spacing` must be at least **1.8×** the letter tracking or it reads as one word.

THE SCALE — and the inversion that makes it read as art-directed
Tight and huge, or tiny and wide-tracked. **Never both.** (Aimé Leon Dore tracks .15em at 10px and 0 at 92px; the reverse is the single loudest template tell.)

| Token | Size | Tracking | Line-height | Case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--t-display-xl` | `clamp(2.75rem, 9.5vw, 6.75rem)` (44→108px) | `-0.02em` | `0.92` | UPPER |
| `--t-display-l` | `clamp(2rem, 5.5vw, 4rem)` (32→64px) | `-0.015em` | `0.98` | UPPER |
| `--t-display-s` | `clamp(1.375rem, 2.6vw, 2rem)` | `-0.01em` | `1.06` | UPPER |
| `--t-body` | `1rem` / `1.0625rem` desktop | `0` | `1.55` | sentence |
| `--t-body-s` | `0.875rem` | `0` | `1.5` | sentence |
| `--t-meta` | `0.625rem` desktop / `0.6875rem` mobile | `0.15em` | `1.4` | UPPER, **Mono** |
| `--t-meta-lg` | `0.75rem` | `0.12em` | `1.3` | UPPER, Mono |

`--t-meta` is the whole metadata layer and it is used a *lot* — datelines, colour names, sizes, prices' currency label, filter chips, the countdown legends. That is the correct home for wide tracking: **labels attached to objects**, never as a decorative eyebrow above every section heading.

NUMERALS: `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on prices, bag counts and countdown digits so nothing jitters. `font-variant-numeric: diagonal-fractions` on the size/measurement table, which carries real half-centimetres. That one line is the detail no template contains.
art_direction.imagery:
**One location world, one light, two people, thirty garments.** The consistency is the luxury.

THE HOUSE LIGHT (identical in every prompt, verbatim, so the site cuts together)
One large soft key from camera left at 45°, **no fill**, shadow falling away to near-black on the subject's right. Outdoors: heavy overcast or the twenty minutes after floodlights come on at dusk. Never golden hour, never rim-lit, never backlit haze.

THE LENS LANGUAGE
35mm for anything with a place in it. 85mm for anything with a garment in it. f/2.8, eye level or slightly below. Graded as **Kodak Portra 400**: fine even grain, slight halation on bone highlights, **matte lifted blacks that land on #0F0F0F, never crushed to #000**. Muted, desaturated, warm-neutral. No HDR, no clarity, no bokeh orbs, no flare.

THE CROP LANGUAGE — this is the casting policy disguised as art direction
Crop at the jaw or above the brow. Backs turned. Three-quarter away. Mid-stride. Hands given a job (in pockets, on a drawcord, gripping a strap). Faces appear front-on in **two frames on the entire site** and both are three-quarter-length at 85mm where the face is a small part of the frame. This is the register a fashion house actually shoots in, *and* it routes around every AI failure mode — small faces, symmetrical features, glassy eyes, plastic skin — without the site ever looking like it is hiding something.

THE PLACE
A single invented-but-specific British world: a municipal athletics track under floodlights after rain; a concrete stairwell with a painted handrail; a plain rendered wall in flat overcast. Wet tarmac. No landmarks, no signage, no other brands, no cars. The place recurs so the drop reads as one afternoon.

THE CAST
**Two models, mid-twenties, deliberately unremarkable faces** (distinctive faces drift less but date the campaign). Each is frozen as a five-view character sheet — front, ¾ left, ¾ right, profile, back-of-head — generated once, one view at a time by editing the previous output, and then used as fixed character-slot references on every subsequent call forever. **Faces approved by the client before a single garment frame is generated.** One variable changes per prompt: same sheet + same garment, change pose; or same sheet + same pose, change garment. Never both.

VIDEO
Ambient forward-play loops only — no scrubbed video anywhere on the site. Fabric moving, a figure walking away, sand. 8 seconds, 24fps, H.264 High, `-an` (audio track stripped entirely, which is stronger than `muted`), a **designed** poster JPEG on every one, `preload="none"` below the fold. Two crops per asset — a native 9:16 and a native 16:9, generated separately, never a centre-crop — served from one element via `<source media="(orientation: portrait)">`.

FLAT-LAYS
The existing renders stay, but only in the product-page media stack and the ledger grid, never in a hero. And garment references fed to the image model are shot **on a hanger or ghost mannequin**, not laid flat — flat-lays have no 3D structure and the model distorts the silhouette to compensate.

WHAT NEVER APPEARS
Smiling at camera. A laptop. A studio strobe highlight. A gradient. An abstract 3D blob. A logo other than OT. Roman numerals anywhere except on the actual pocket print of the actual garment. The tessellated OT pattern as a page background — it appears once, on the Story page, at low contrast, cropped hard, and never behind text.
art_direction.motion:
**Three permitted motions. Everything else is static. This is a rule, enforced in review, not a preference.**

**1. The slow hand.** A raking specular highlight on the glass pill's 1px rim, driven by *page scroll progress*, completing exactly one 360° revolution from the top of the document to the bottom. One `@property --ot-light` angle, one conic-gradient ring, one rAF-coalesced scroll handler writing one custom property. Works in every browser, costs nothing, and it is the only clock on the site — abstract, peripheral, and impossible to read as a gimmick because it never tells you a time.
```css
@property --ot-light{syntax:'<angle>';inherits:false;initial-value:210deg}
```

**2. The settle.** Editorial images and display lines arrive with `opacity 0→1` and `translateY(14px→0)` over **900ms** on `--ot-ease: cubic-bezier(.16,.84,.24,1)` — heavy, decelerating, expensive-feeling. Fires **once** per element. **Maximum one settle per viewport.** No stagger. No 100ms increments. If two things would settle together, one of them doesn't move. Implemented as native `animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports` (compositor-thread, ~0ms INP) with a 15-line IntersectionObserver fallback for Firefox. Baseline state is *visible* — content is never hidden behind an animation that might not run.

**3. The sequence.** The one pinned canvas moment, at the bottom of the home page. 120 WebP frames, 260vh runway, ~11px of scroll per frame on desktop and ~8px on mobile. This is the entire motion budget for the site, spent in one place, which is what makes it read as intentional.

RESTRAINT RULES (the ban list, and it is enforceable)
- Nothing parallaxes except the single depth-mapped location plate, at ±0.012 UV offset, scroll-driven only, desktop + `pointer: fine` only, disabled under Save-Data and reduced-motion. If you can consciously see it, turn it down.
- No page-transition library, no smooth-scroll library (**no Lenis** — it fights native scroll timelines, adds input latency by design, and overrides the user's OS scroll settings).
- No custom cursor. No tilt. No count-ups. No typewriter. No marquee. No scroll-progress bar. No stagger. No hover state that changes nothing.
- Durations are **640ms / 900ms / 1400ms**. Nothing is 200ms except the nav theme flip and the gel press.
- Buttons and the pill's items press with a `linear()` spring (`scale(.955) scaleY(.93)`, 520ms) — the one place the motion is fast, because touch feedback must be immediate.

REDUCED MOTION is total, not cosmetic: the global `*` override neutralises `animation-timeline: auto`, the sequence renders **one chosen frame at ~62% progress** (not frame 1 — the best-composed frame), the WebGL depth plate never initialises, the specular freezes at 210°, and the hero video loses `autoplay` and gains visible controls. WCAG 2.2.2 (Level A) governs the autoplaying loop; this is a legal-exposure item for a commercial storefront, not a nicety.

page_by_page.name: COVER (home, spread 00)
page_by_page.purpose: Establish that this is a publication, not a shop front. Sell the light, the place and the tee. Say 'EARN EVERY SECOND.' once and never again. Zero buttons — the pill is the only affordance on screen.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** 100vw × 100svh, a single ambient video bleeding to all four edges. No container, no max-width, no centring. Bottom-left, inside a 56px gutter: a three-line mono dateline in `--t-meta` / #A7A5A4 — `OUR TIME` / `DROP 01 — PHOTOGRAPHED 09.26` / `NORTH TRACK, 19:40 BST`. Directly beneath it, flush left, `EARN EVERY SECOND.` in `--t-display-xl` (108px), bone, tracking -0.02em, line-height 0.92, breaking to two lines. Bottom-right, a single mono line `SCROLL` with a 24px hairline beneath it — no arrow, no bounce. Nothing else. The glass pill floats 20px from the top, centred, over the darkest third of the frame. **Mobile:** the native 9:16 cut, 100vw × 100svh (`svh`, not `vh`, so the URL bar does not cause CLS). Dateline and display line stack at the bottom in the 16px gutter, display clamps to 44px over two lines. `SCROLL` is dropped — it is desktop chrome. Pill is 232px, centred, 14px from the top.
page_by_page.media: OT-COVER-VID-16x9 and OT-COVER-VID-9x16 — two natively generated 8s loops, never a centre-crop of each other. Model A, back to camera, mid-stride, walking away down a wet floodlit municipal running track at dusk in the navy hourglass tee and washed grey shorts. The hourglass back-print is fully readable for the first 3 seconds and the figure recedes. Fabric moves; nothing else does. Generated via Veo 3.1 Fast image-to-video with the same still passed as both `image` and `lastFrame` so it loops seamlessly with no crossfade. Poster = a designed frame at t≈1.2s, AVIF.
page_by_page.interaction: `<video autoplay muted loop playsinline preload="metadata">` with `<source media="(orientation: portrait)">` first so the browser picks the phone cut natively with no JS and no double download. `data-nav-theme="video"` on the section → the pill cross-fades to opaque for its duration (no blur over moving video). Nothing animates in on load; the page is simply already there. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the video is replaced by its poster with visible controls.

page_by_page.name: SPREAD 01 — THE TEE
page_by_page.purpose: The hero garment, at full editorial scale. Establish the asymmetric off-grid language: image bleeds off one edge, type sits in a narrow column, nothing is centred.
page_by_page.layout: Dark ground. **Desktop:** 12-column grid, 24px gutters, 56px page margin *except where an image bleeds*. The image occupies columns 1–7 and **bleeds off the left edge of the viewport**, 88svh tall, `aspect-ratio` unconstrained (object-fit cover), cropped so the top of the hourglass print runs off the top of the frame. Columns 9–12 hold, aligned to the image's lower third: a mono dateline; a 48-word paragraph in `--t-body` at a 34ch measure; a mono spec block (`340 GSM · GARMENT-DYED · OVERSIZED · BOX FIT`); and a single text link, `NAVY / HOURGLASS — £68`, underlined 1px at 6px offset. **No button.** Column 8 is left empty — the visible gap is the design. **Mobile:** image goes full-bleed edge to edge at `aspect-ratio: 4/5`, then a 32px gap, then the text block in the 16px gutter, left-aligned, in the same order. The link becomes a 48px-tall tap row with a hairline above and below.
page_by_page.media: OT-TEE-BACK — on-model, back to camera, 4:5 portrait, the navy #141B2C oversized washed tee with the full distressed-engraving hourglass back-print in bone ink, cropped at mid-neck so the head is out of frame. Shot at 85mm against the near-black studio sweep with the house light from camera left.
page_by_page.interaction: The image settles once (900ms, --ot-ease, 14px rise) on `animation-timeline: view()` with `animation-range: entry 10% cover 30%`. The text column does **not** settle — only one thing moves per viewport. The link's underline thickens from 1px to 1px + a 1px denim rule beneath on hover; no colour change, no translate.

page_by_page.name: SPREAD 02 — THE RUN
page_by_page.purpose: Show the six sweat-short colourways as one family without turning them into a card grid. This is the spread that proves the range architecture exists.
page_by_page.layout: Dark ground. **Desktop:** six frames on a 3-column grid, `aspect-ratio: 83/100` (derived from the actual flat-lay crop, not a round number — off-grid ratios are half of what makes a page look art-directed). Alternating columns are pushed **down by 64px**, so the baselines stagger; the first and last frames in each row bleed 56px past the page margin into the gutter. Under each frame, a mono caption only: the colour name, then a 1px × 18px rule in that colour, then `£46`. No add-to-bag on this spread — it is editorial, and the reader goes to the ledger to buy. Headline `TIME WON'T WAIT.` in `--t-display-l` sits in the empty slot created by the stagger, not above the grid. **Mobile:** 2-up, `83/100`, 12px gutter, **no vertical stagger** (it reads as a bug at narrow widths), captions beneath, the headline above the grid at 32px.
page_by_page.media: OT-SHORTS-RUN — six on-model frames, same model, same pose, same light, one colourway each: washed grey #A7A5A4, washed denim #54647E, off-white #DFDDDE, cream/sand #CFC2B4, washed black #171717, navy #141925. Cropped from the ribcage to mid-calf — no face, so identity drift is structurally impossible across six frames. Hands: one in the pocket, one on the drawcord, fingers separated and visible. **Washed black and off-white are shot on the mid-grey sweep, not the near-black**, because #171717 dies on #0F0F0F.
page_by_page.interaction: The grid reveals as **one** settle on the container, not six staggered children. Colour captions are plain text, not swatch chips — chips in a row is a component-library tell. Tapping a frame goes to that colourway's product URL directly (`/shorts-washed-denim`), not to a filtered grid.

page_by_page.name: SPREAD 03 — THE PLATE
page_by_page.purpose: Breathing room. One image, no type, no product, no purpose beyond confidence. This is the beat that separates a lookbook from a catalogue, and it is where the '3D flair' lives — as depth, not as a scene graph.
page_by_page.layout: **Desktop:** 100vw × 78svh, full-bleed, zero type, zero UI. Hard cut into it from the dark ground above and hard cut out of it below — no fade, no rounded corners, no inner margin. **Mobile:** 100vw × 62svh. Identical treatment. On both, a single mono dateline sits in the very bottom-left corner at 16px/56px inset, #A7A5A4 at 60% opacity — the only mark on the frame.
page_by_page.media: OT-PLATE-TRACK — an empty floodlit municipal athletics track at dusk after rain, no people, wet tarmac reflecting the floodlight columns, overcast sky going to slate. 35mm, f/2.8. Plus OT-PLATE-DEPTH: a greyscale depth map baked offline with Depth Anything V2, hand-touched in Photoshop where the track edge meets the sky, shipped as a half-resolution greyscale WebP (~10–14KB).
page_by_page.interaction: ~60 lines of raw WebGL (no Three.js — 185KB gzipped and 400–700ms of main-thread parse before a pixel, for an effect we can fake at 4KB) displacing UVs by the depth map, 6 refinement iterations, `uOffset` driven from scroll progress only at **±0.012**. The image appears to have a few centimetres of real depth as you pass it. Desktop + `pointer: fine` only; never initialises on `saveData`, `effectiveType` 2g/3g, or `prefers-reduced-motion` — in all those cases it is simply a very good photograph, which was always the point.

page_by_page.name: SPREAD 04 — THE INDEX (the light section)
page_by_page.purpose: The collection entry point, as a typographic index rather than a grid of 'shop by category' cards. This is the only light section on the home page, and it is what forces — and therefore justifies — the glass pill's adaptive flip.
page_by_page.layout: `--ot-paper` #DFDDDE ground, `--ot-ink-dark` #141B2C ink, `data-nav-theme="light"`. **Desktop:** left half (cols 1–6) is a vertical list of seven rows, one per garment type, each a full-width flex row: garment name in `--t-display-s` (32px, navy, uppercase, tracking -0.01em) on the left, and on the right a mono count — `SWEAT SHORTS ······ 6 COLOURWAYS`. 1px `--ot-rule-light` between rows, 28px row padding. Right half (cols 8–12) holds a single 4:5 image that **swaps** to match whichever row is hovered/focused, with a 240ms crossfade and a mono caption beneath it. Default state shows the tee. **Mobile:** the list is the whole section, rows are 64px tall tap targets; tapping a row expands it inline (a `<details>`-backed disclosure) to reveal a 2-up thumbnail pair and a `VIEW ALL →` link, pushing the rows below down. No hover-dependent content on touch.
page_by_page.media: OT-INDEX-THUMBS — seven 4:5 stills, one per garment type (tee, polo, crewneck, zip hoodie, sweat shorts, sweatpants, baggy jeans), all on Model B, all the same three-quarter-away crop, all the same light. They are deliberately near-identical apart from the garment, because that is what makes the index read as a catalogue of one thing rather than seven moods.
page_by_page.interaction: Row hover / focus-visible swaps the image (desktop). Every row is a real `<a>` to `/shop/<handle>` — the whole spread works with JS disabled and with a keyboard. The nav pill flips to `data-over="light"` as this section crosses its band and flips back on exit; that transition is 200ms and is the only colour transition on the site.

page_by_page.name: SPREAD 05 — THE GLASS (the one sequence)
page_by_page.purpose: The structural payoff. The entire motion budget, spent once, on the brand's best asset. The hourglass's lower bulb fills as you scroll — accrual, not depletion — and the page's last line is the brand's name.
page_by_page.layout: Pinned section, **260vh** runway, `position: sticky; top: 0; height: 100svh` inner. Transitions from paper back to ground: the sequence's frames are rendered on #0F0F0F so the section cut is invisible. The hourglass is **not centred** — it sits at 38% from the left on desktop, filling 82% of viewport height, cropped so the top bulb runs off the top edge and only the lower bulb and the falling stream are in frame. Right side, vertically centred, a mono progress dateline that increments in real units as you scroll (`00:00:00` → `00:04:00`, tabular-nums) — the one place a duration is displayed, and it is a *record of the render*, not a clock. At the end of the pin, `OUR TIME.` settles in at `--t-display-xl` in bone, flush left at the 56px margin, and the pin releases. **Mobile:** hourglass centred, 72% of viewport height, the duration readout drops (too small to read, too precious to shrink), `OUR TIME.` at 44px over two lines.
page_by_page.media: OT-HOURGLASS-SEQ — **Blender, rendered offline, not an API asset.** Cycles, orthographic-ish 50mm, the OUR TIME hourglass modelled from the back-print engraving: aged brass frame, slightly cloudy glass, sand at #CFC2B4. The house light from camera left, no fill, on #0F0F0F. 120 frames at 30fps = 4 seconds of sand accumulating in the lower bulb, with the stream continuous throughout. time_theme:
Seven structural expressions, none of them decorative. If you deleted every hourglass and clock illustration from the site, six of these would survive.

**1. Time is the metadata layer.** Every image on the site carries a mono dateline in `--t-meta` — `DROP 01 — PHOTOGRAPHED 09.26 / NORTH TRACK, 19:40 BST`. Every product carries `MADE 08.26 · DROP 01`. The dates are real. This is how a magazine handles time (datelines and issue numbers) and it gives the wide-tracked 10px mono type — the one place tracking belongs — a genuine job. It also happens to be the anti-vibe-code lint's #55 ("no real numbers, no real dates, no real place names anywhere") answered head-on.

**2. The collection is sorted by time before it is sorted by anything else.** `/shop` defaults to chronological — newest first, a ledger. Style, colour and size are *filters applied on top of that order*. Category-first IA is what every Shopify theme does; time-first IA is a structural claim about what the brand thinks matters, and it scales cleanly to drop 02, 03, 04.

**3. The page is the arc of the corrected name.** The cover says `EARN EVERY SECOND.` The middle says `TIME WON'T WAIT.` The closing spread, after 260vh of sand, says `OUR TIME.` — once, and nowhere else on the site. Grind, then arrival. The brand holds both halves of its meaning and you cannot reach the second without scrolling through the first. That arc only became available when the name was corrected from OVERTIME to OUR TIME, which is the most direct possible proof that the design is built on *this* brand and not a generic streetwear template.

**4. The sequence fills rather than empties.** The one canvas moment is the hourglass's **lower bulb accumulating**, not the top draining. Depletion is anxiety; accrual is earning. It is the same physical object as the tee's back-print, cropped differently, so the site's structural climax and the range's hero graphic are literally the same asset viewed from a different framing.

**5. The specular sweep is one hand, one revolution, one page.** `--ot-light` is driven from document scroll progress, 0→360°, so the highlight crosses the glass pill's rim exactly once between the top and the bottom of the page. It is the only clock on the site and it never tells you a time — it tells you how much is left. Abstract enough that nobody will name it, present enough that the page feels like it is keeping time. It is also the concept's name.

**6. Two timers, two registers — which is what stops the countdown reading as a gimmick.** The drop page carries **one** countdown, Corteiz-inverted so it counts to the drop *closing* (scarcity you can act on, not a wait). The footer and the cart carry a **dispatch cut-off** — `ORDER BY 14:00 BST FOR SAME-DAY DISPATCH` — which is pure service information. Hype and utility, side by side, both true. A brand with only the first is selling urgency; a brand with both is running a business.

**7. The copy is collective and it is about hours, not moments.** "OUR" is a we. The connective writing never says "you". It says things like *we made this in the hours nobody pays for* — the register of shared, unglamorous, accumulated time, which is what "overtime into our time" actually means and what `DISCIPLINE. FOCUS. CONSISTENCY.` already states in the brand's own words.

**Explicitly refused**, because each is the first thing anyone thinks of and therefore the first thing everyone builds: a ticking-clock cursor; a live current-time readout in the header; an hourglass loading spinner; a sand-particle canvas background; a second-hand sweep as a scroll-progress indicator; Roman numerals used as UI (they belong on the pocket print, which is where they work); an SVG clock face as a hero graphic; the tessellated OT monogram as a page background; and `OUR TIME` set as an H1 over a centred hero with two buttons. The slogan is strong. That arrangement is the tell.

tech_stack:
**Astro 5, TypeScript, hand-written CSS, two adapters, one dependency.**

**Framework — Astro 5.** Zero JS shipped by default, which matters more than anything else here: this site is 90% static editorial and 10% interactive, and Astro is the only mainstream framework whose default is "ship nothing". Product and collection pages are statically generated from the catalogue at build time (real, indexable, cacheable `<html>` — a client-only SPA would be an SEO own-goal for a storefront), with islands only where interaction genuinely exists: the nav pill, the cart drawer, the filter bar, the PDP variant selector, the sequence. If the Shopify decision later requires a **private** Storefront token (which it will, the moment site content moves into metaobjects), flip on the Node or Cloudflare adapter and SSR those routes — a one-line config change, not a rewrite. That escape hatch is why Astro and not a pure SSG.

**Styling — plain CSS with custom properties and `@layer`. Explicitly not Tailwind.** Not purism: Tailwind's *defaults* are the tell. `rounded-2xl p-6 shadow-lg bg-white/10 backdrop-blur-md border border-white/20 py-24` is the exact fingerprint of a generated site, and the gravitational pull of a utility scale is towards those values. The whole point of this direction is `border-radius: 0` everywhere except two max-pills, no shadows except the pill's cast, an off-grid `83/100` aspect ratio, and a bespoke `clamp()` type scale. Hand-written tokens make the deliberate choices visible in the source and the accidental ones impossible. ~900 lines of CSS total.

**No UI framework.** Nav, drawer, filter bar and variant selector are vanilla custom elements (~60–120 lines each) with progressive enhancement — `<details>`, real `<a>` hrefs, real `<form>` posts underneath. Everything works with JS disabled.

**The one dependency — GSAP ScrollTrigger (~27KB gz), dynamically imported, for the one pinned section only.** Pinning is genuinely hard (scrollbar compensation, resize, `refresh()` on layout change, iOS rubber-band) and this is the single place a library earns its bytes. GSAP became 100% free in April 2025 under Webflow, all plugins included, commercial use permitted — **but "free" is not "open source"; read `node_modules/gsap/LICENSE.md` before shipping a commercial storefront.** It is a 30-second check and it is a client project.

**No Lenis, no Locomotive, no Framer Motion, no Three.js, no Swiper.** Lenis hijacks native scroll, breaks `animation-timeline: scroll()`, adds input latency by design, and overrides the user's OS scroll settings. Three.js is 185KB gz and 400–700ms of main-thread parse before a pixel, for an effect we deliver in 60 lines of raw WebGL at ~4KB. Across eleven teardown sites, not one referenced any of these — the category ships video, IntersectionObserver and native CSS scroll timelines, and so do we.

**Scroll motion — native CSS first.** `animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports` (Chrome/Edge 115+, **Safari 26+ since Sept 2025**, Firefox still behind `layout.css.scroll-driven-animations.enabled` in Release), with a 15-line IntersectionObserver fallback. These run on the compositor thread and cost essentially **0ms of INP**; a GSAP scrub costs a main-thread tick per frame. Not Baseline yet, and `animation-range` is unimplemented in Firefox even behind the flag — so it is enhancement, never the baseline, and content is visible by default.

**Images and video.** AVIF for every static still (best bytes). **WebP for the sequence frames** — AVIF decode is 5–10× slower than JPEG and that is irrelevant for one hero image and *the entire bottleneck* for 120 sequential decodes on a mid-range Android. Product media stays in the Shopify CDN once it exists, so the cousin can upload it himself; hero and lookbook video goes to Cloudflare Stream or pre-encoded MP4+WebM on the host CDN, not Shopify Files.

**Hosting — Cloudflare Pages or Netlify.** Free tier is genuinely sufficient at launch. HTTP/2+ is mandatory for the 120-frame sequence (on HTTP/1.1 the 6-connection limit makes it a disaster); any modern CDN gives it free.

---

**THE COMMERCE SEAM — the actual point of the architecture**

Two seams, because most of this site is not commerce.

```
components → useCommerce() → StorefrontAdapter → local-json | shopify | stripe
           → useContent()  → ContentAdapter   → local-json | metaobjects | sanity
```

**Ship v1 on `createLocalAdapter()` reading `content/catalogue.json`.** Design and build start today with zero platform risk. Seven non-negotiable rules keep the seam real rather than aspirational:
1. No Shopify type and no `gid://shopify/…` string ever appears in a component. IDs are opaque branded strings.
2. Money is **never** a JS number in the UI — `{amountMinor: 4600, currencyCode: 'GBP'}`, one `formatMoney()`.
3. URLs key on **handle**, never on ID.
4. The front-end never computes tax, shipping or totals. It renders what the cart returns.
5. Exactly one file knows `SHOPIFY_API_VERSION = "2026-07"`.
6. Adapters return typed `CartResult`s for user-visible failures; they throw only for programmer errors.
7. **Both adapters pass the same conformance suite** — sparse variant matrices, display-ordered option values, `compareAtPrice` null-or-greater, `quantity 0` removes the line, line attributes survive a round trip, `beginCheckout` on an empty cart returns `{kind:'unavailable'}`. When the Shopify adapter goes green, the swap is done. That suite is the entire insurance policy and it costs about a day.

**Do NOT build Hydrogen/Oxygen.** It is the maximum-lock-in option — coupled to Shopify's framework *and* hosting *and* opinions — and its framework has been rewritten under its users twice (RSC → Remix → React Router). It buys nothing a plain front-end doesn't have.

**Modelled now, on fake data, because faking them wrongly forces a redesign later:** variants as the sellable unit; sparse size×colour matrices ("doesn't exist" ≠ "sold out"); tri-state inventory (`false` / `3` / `null` — treating null as 0 is the classic bug); editorial option ordering (S/M/L/XL is not alphabetical); `compareAtPrice`; media galleries as a union of image/video/3D in merchant order with variant association (**video-native from the first commit**, because the AI loops and the flat-lays live in the same gallery); collections as first-class objects with handles and SEO, not tag filters; cart lines with their own IDs and attributes; server-validated discount codes that can fail; and checkout as an **always-a-redirect** handoff.

**Practical sequencing.** Open a Shopify store now on the £1-for-3-months intro, load the real seven styles and ~31 colourways, and generate `catalogue.json` *from* it — so the cousin starts learning the admin (which is where 90% of his daily work lives, path-independently) while the site is still being designed, and so we are building against real data rather than invented data. Interim `beginCheckout` returns a **cart permalink** (`https://<shop>.myshopify.com/cart/<variantId>:1`) — a fully bespoke PDP handing off to a real Shopify cart with zero SDK, zero token and zero API surface. That is an underrated launch mode and it means he can take money before the platform decision is formally made.

**The one honest gate.** If the cousin turns out to want to re-lay-out home-page sections himself, weekly, a custom Liquid theme genuinely wins and we should re-cost it *before* building the ContentAdapter. Ask him that question in week one, not in month three.

**Ongoing:** bump one API-version constant each quarter (~1 hour), and brand the hosted checkout in Shopify's checkout editor — logo, #141B2C, #DFDDDE, matching type — because below Plus that is the only control we have over the last three screens, and the softness of that handoff is worth an afternoon.
anti_vibe_code:
Run against the 61-point tells checklist. Every item below is a decision that costs something and that a generated site would not make.

**Colour — 7 of 7 clear.** No gradient exists anywhere on the site, on any surface, in any state. No hue is introduced that isn't already on a garment — the single accent is `#54647E`, the washed denim, and it is confined to three named uses. Ink on paper is **navy `#141B2C`, not black**, which is the one colour decision that separates a fashion house from a theme. Tokens are material-named (`--ot-ground`, `--ot-paper-warm`, `--ot-denim`), never `--primary/--secondary/--accent`. Backgrounds are `#0F0F0F` and `#DFDDDE` — both measured off the client's own renders — not `slate-900` and not `#FFFFFF`. No coloured glow under anything.

**Typography — the inversion, and one face.** Tracking is `0` at 108px and `.15em` at 10px, never the reverse. Wide tracking appears only on **labels attached to objects** (a colour name, a size, a date, a SKU), never as a decorative eyebrow above every heading. One superfamily in three registers (Söhne / Söhne Schmal / Söhne Mono), four styles, one italic — and the italic is the OT monogram itself, not a font. Inter, Poppins, Montserrat and the whole Google top-20 are banned by name in the stylesheet comment. Every size is a bespoke `clamp()`, not a Tailwind step. **The wordmark is outlined SVG, not type**, and the two places it must be live type carry explicit `word-spacing: .62em` against `letter-spacing: .34em` — a 1.8× ratio — because the corrections flagged the word space as the fragile part and a default will collapse it.

**Layout — the refusals.** There is no centred hero with a headline, a subhead and two buttons; the cover has **no buttons at all**. There is no three-up feature grid, no Features/Testimonials/FAQ/CTA rhythm, no stats band, no logo strip, no numbered step timeline, no badge pill above an H1, no marquee, no four-equal-column footer. Vertical rhythm is set per spread by the image, not by a global `py-24`. Images bleed off the viewport edge on three of seven home spreads and column 8 of the twelve is left deliberately empty on spread 01 — the visible gap *is* the design. Aspect ratios are `4/5`, `1/1`, `21/9` and **`83/100`**, the last derived from an actual flat-lay crop rather than from a round number, which is the ALD `69/50` move.

**Radius and shadow — commit to a pole.** Everything on the site is `border-radius: 0`. The two glass surfaces are `2147483647px`. Nothing is 8px, 12px or 16px. There is exactly **one** `box-shadow` in the entire stylesheet — the nav pill's cast — and zero shadows on cards, buttons or containers. No `border: 1px solid white/10` wrapper on anything; hairlines are `rgb(250 246 246 / .14)` and they separate rows, not enclose boxes.

**Glass — one surface per viewport, and it is load-bearing.** No glass cards, no glass modals, no `backdrop-blur` on anything that isn't the nav pill or the collection filter bar. The adaptive light/dark flip is not a flourish: the arithmetic (`.78` dark scrim over `#DFDDDE` → bone ink at **3.8:1**, failing) forces it, and I've shown the working. Chromatic aberration is deliberately omitted — RGB fringing reads as glitch and fights a washed, desaturated, vintage-athletic brand.

**Motion — three permitted movements, and a ban list.** One settle per viewport, never a stagger, never in tidy 100ms increments. No custom cursor, no tilt, no count-up, no typewriter, no scroll-progress bar, no page-wide parallax, no smooth-scroll library. Durations are 640/900/1400ms on a heavy custom ease, not 200ms snaps. `prefers-reduced-motion` is total — it kills the sequence, the WebGL plate, the specular and video autoplay, and it is wired for `prefers-contrast`, `forced-colors` and `prefers-reduced-transparency` too (the last of which Safari does not support, which is precisely why the scrim floor is a locked token rather than a preference-dependent nicety).

**Imagery and copy.** No AI person smiles at camera. Faces appear front-on in two frames on the whole site, both three-quarter-length at 85mm. Skin is prompted as "natural matte skin with visible pores and real texture" rather than as "not plastic". Garments are shown worn, in a place, in one recurring light — flat-lays live in the grid and the PDP stack, never in a hero. Copy uses the brand's own confirmed lines and the collective "we"; there is no "elevate your everyday", no "where style meets comfort", no invented testimonial, no filler. Every image caption carries a real date and a real place.

**Five specific details no template contains, and each is cheap:**
1. `font-variant-numeric: diagonal-fractions` on the size chart, which carries real half-centimetres.
2. `:has(.ot-countdown){visibility:hidden}` guarding the drop hero, so nobody ever sees a flash of `00:00:00`, and an in-place swap to a live link on expiry instead of dead zeros.
3. A `bg: dark | paper` field on every catalogue colourway, because washed grey `#A7A5A4` is 1.84:1 against paper and washed black `#171717` is 8 luminance points from the ground — the palette maths dictates where a garment is allowed to be photographed and displayed, and the CMS enforces it.
4. Two timers in two registers — a drop-*closing* countdown and a dispatch cut-off — so urgency and service sit side by side and neither reads as an app.
5. A mobile nav pill that is 232px wide because a smaller blurred area is both the cheaper render and the more premium look — a performance constraint and an aesthetic one pointing the same way, taken as a design decision rather than a compromise.

**The test every decision is held against:** *would this exist if the brand had a full-time art director and no AI tools?* Corteiz's 12px yellow Courier passes. A ticking-clock cursor does not.
risks: **Restraint has no floor under it if the photography isn't excellent.** Aimé Leon Dore gets away with a 78svh plate carrying no type because the photograph is worth 78svh. At a $15 pilot, generated by a model with documented consistency weaknesses, it might not be. If the hero frames come back merely competent, this direction reads as empty rather than expensive — and empty is the one failure mode with no cheap fix, because the response (adding sections, adding copy, adding cards) destroys the concept. **Gate:** OT-TEE-BACK and OT-PLATE-TRACK must both clear client QA before any layout is built. If either fails twice, re-cost the direction rather than proceeding.

**The pinned canvas sequence sits directly under a fixed glass pill — the research's explicitly named worst case.** `position: fixed` + `backdrop-filter` defeats WebKit's blur cache on every scroll frame, and a per-frame canvas repaint means the backdrop is dirty every frame. The mitigation (the pill goes opaque for the duration of the pin) works, but it means the site's signature effect is switched off during the site's signature moment. That is a genuine loss, not a clever solve, and the client should be told so before it ships.

**The client asked for liquid glass and will almost certainly view the site on an iPhone, where Tier 1 refraction renders nothing at all.** `backdrop-filter: url(#svg-filter)` is Chromium-only; WebKit bug 245510 is still NEW and PR #68614 is open and `merging-blocked`; on iOS every browser is WebKit so there is no escape hatch. He will see a very good blur and may reasonably say "that isn't what Apple does." This is a project-management risk, not a technical one, and it is the single most likely source of disappointment on the whole build. Show him Tier 2 on his own phone in week one, before the design is signed off.

**Chronological-default collection sort is elegant and might be wrong for the actual shopper.** With seven styles and ~31 colourways, a customer who wants "shorts, medium, cream" is not served by a ledger — they are served by a filter. The whole architecture therefore leans on the sticky filter bar carrying real load, and if it is under-built (no multi-select, no URL state, no fast mobile sheet), the time-first IA stops reading as a considered position and starts reading as pretentious. Budget the filter bar as a first-class component, not as chrome.

**The palette's own arithmetic removes flexibility we may later want.** Washed grey `#A7A5A4` is 1.84:1 against the paper theme and washed black `#171717` is eight luminance points from the ground — so two of the six shorts colourways can only ever appear on one of the two site themes. That is a real constraint on every future grid, editorial spread and social crop, and it will be discovered again and again by whoever maintains the site unless the `bg` field is enforced in the catalogue schema from day one.

**The hourglass sequence requires Blender competence and a 120-frame Cycles render, and the client was told Blender was overkill.** Here it is load-bearing: it is the entire motion budget, the structural climax of the time theme, and the payoff line's stage. If nobody renders it, spreads 05 and the `OUR TIME.` payoff both evaporate and the home page becomes a nice grid with a good footer. There is no cheap substitute — an AI-generated video of an hourglass will not hold a frame-accurate scrub and will not match the engraving.

**Identity drift across ~30 on-model frames is the documented weak point of the chosen image model**, and this direction needs more consistency than most because the whole conceit is "one afternoon, one light, two people". DeepMind's own model page says character consistency "may not always get it right". The five-view character sheet plus one-variable-per-prompt discipline is the mitigation, but it turns a shoot into a QA job, and the rejection rate — not the API spend — is the real cost. Two models is already the maximum; a third would double QA for no commercial gain.

**This direction fails in revision, not in design.** There is nothing to add. If the cousin comes back asking for more energy, more product above the fold, a testimonial section or a bigger logo, every available response breaks the concept — and unlike a busier direction, there is no slack to absorb one bad note. The counter-argument (that Fear of God ships three heroes and a footer) only holds for brands with existing demand; OUR TIME has none yet, and `EST. 2026` in the footer says so. Time-to-product on the home page is one full screen, which is confident for Palace and unproven for a launch.

**The globe tee carries 41.8781 N, 87.6298 W — Chicago.** If the brand is not Chicago-based this is a stray detail on a real garment, and it will end up in product copy, alt text and the lookbook caption unless someone asks. The site's whole dateline system depends on real places being real. **Open question for the client, not a design decision:** is this deliberate, and if not, is the garment being reprinted or is the site simply never naming the coordinates?

**The two source briefs disagree about the range.** The corrections confirm seven garment types and ~31 colourways and demand a genuine collection architecture; a later line says design for the navy hourglass tee and the six sweat-short colourways only. I have built the architecture for seven (the ledger, the index spread, the filter bar, the sparse variant matrix) and art-directed the home page around the tee and the shorts run, because those are the pieces that exist as approved renders and carry the theme. If the intent was genuinely a one-drop capsule, spread 04 (The Index) and roughly a third of the collection build are over-engineering and should be cut before work starts — worth resolving in the first conversation rather than the fifth.
